strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: generating 3D geometry from VR sketches while preserving stroke structure. The combination of an automatic sketch synthesis pipeline, 20,838 synthetic pairs, and 900 human-drawn sketches across four categories is a meaningful contribution beyond the model architecture.

Table 2 shows substantial improvements under matched synthetic-training and real-fine-tuning protocols on the proposed dataset: F-score increases from 48.8 to 69.8 and CD×1000 decreases from 13.0 to 4.8 relative to Luo et al. Gains also hold on the external 3DVRChair benchmark, with F-score improving from 26.6 to 31.1 and CD decreasing from 35.5 to 25.8.

The zero-shot ablations provide useful evidence for the representation and training pipeline. The full model achieves 56.8 F-score versus 48.9 without sequence indices, 49.0 without augmentation, and 30.8 with point-cloud encoding. Figure 4 also shows visibly improved structural fidelity across several categories.

The method is clearly organized and largely technically plausible. Encoder dimensions, optimization settings, synthesis thresholds, and runtime are reported. Synthetic-to-real adaptation and partial-input experiments add practical value beyond full-sketch reconstruction.
weaknesses: The central claim about temporal drawing order is not isolated. The 'w/o stroke ordering' ablation removes both stroke and within-stroke point indices, thereby removing stroke identity and local connectivity information as well as chronology. Its performance drop supports structured sequence encoding, but does not establish that human temporal order itself is responsible. A shuffled-stroke comparison preserving stroke membership and within-stroke connectivity is missing, as is a comparison against geometric ordering of real sketches.

Shape-level separation between synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation is unspecified. All are derived from ShapeNet, but the manuscript does not establish whether evaluation meshes were excluded from synthetic sketch generation. Participant separation is also unreported. This is not evidence of leakage, but it prevents assessing whether the reported transfer reflects generalization to unseen geometry and drawing styles.

The new human dataset consists of tracing visible reference models with every point snapped onto the target surface. This is a useful controlled benchmark, but it differs substantially from freehand ideation without an existing target mesh. The lower sketch-to-shape distance in Table 1 follows directly from this collection procedure and does not independently validate realistic sketch quality. External 3DVRChair results partly address this concern, but broad claims about real-world design workflows remain insufficiently supported.

Some evaluation details limit reproducibility and interpretation. Figure 5 labels its horizontal axis as samples per category up to 200, although only chairs have 200 fine-tuning examples; the evaluated category scope is unclear. The manuscript also leaves sequence resampling/length handling and several synthetic stroke-ordering details unspecified. Partial completion pads the missing suffix with MASK tokens, but does not explain how its length would be determined from an actual unfinished sketch.

Overall, the dataset effort and consistent reconstruction gains make this a credible contribution near the acceptance boundary. However, the unresolved split protocol and the confounding of temporal order with structural encoding directly affect the interpretation of its main scientific claims. These material uncertainties balance the positive evidence and motivate a borderline assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem with a substantial combined contribution: an automatic sketch synthesis pipeline, 20,838 synthetic and 900 human-drawn sketch–shape pairs across four categories, and a sequential sketch-conditioned shape generator.

Table 2 reports meaningful improvements over retrained baselines. Across the new dataset, F-score increases from 48.8 to 69.8 and CD×1000 decreases from 13.0 to 4.8 relative to Luo et al. Improvements also hold on the external 3DVRChair benchmark, where F-score rises from 26.6 to 31.1 and CD decreases from 35.5 to 25.8. Figure 4 provides visually consistent evidence of better structural reconstruction.

The synthetic-to-real results are promising: the synthetic-only chair model achieves 56.8 F-score, and relatively little real-data adaptation improves performance further. Table 3 also supports the usefulness of augmentation and the proposed representation compared with PointNet++ conditioning.

The architecture is understandable and technically plausible. The manuscript specifies encoder dimensions, training schedules, several synthesis thresholds, and inference costs, and acknowledges the limitations imposed by the frozen, low-resolution shape autoencoder.
weaknesses: The central claim about temporal drawing order is not cleanly established. The 'w/o stroke ordering' ablation removes both stroke and within-stroke point indices. This simultaneously removes temporal order and information identifying stroke membership and polyline connectivity. Consequently, the improvement from 48.9 to 56.8 F-score does not isolate natural drawing order. A control that preserves stroke structure while permuting stroke order, alongside separate point-order and stroke-order ablations, is missing.

The new real sketches are traced over visible target meshes and projected onto their surfaces. This is a useful controlled benchmark, but it differs materially from freehand ideation without an existing target. The reduced sketch-to-shape distance in Table 1 follows directly from snapping and does not independently demonstrate greater usefulness for realistic sketch-conditioned generation. External-benchmark gains partially address this concern, but synthetic-only transfer to unsnapped sketches is not established.

Dataset separation is insufficiently documented. The manuscript gives sketch split sizes but does not specify whether target ShapeNet objects are disjoint between synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation, or whether participants are held out. This does not establish leakage, but it prevents determining whether the reported generalization includes unseen shapes and drawing styles.

The partial-sketch protocol pads the unobserved remainder with MASK tokens and randomly inserts separators, without explaining how the unknown final sequence length and stroke structure would be determined during live drawing. Thus, Figures 6–7 support completion under the stated simulation more clearly than the claimed interactive workflow.

Some experimental details remain ambiguous: Figure 5 includes 200 real samples per category although only chairs have that many fine-tuning examples, and the stated zero-shot ablation setting has an unexplained real-trained exception. The diffusion description also leaves the precise prediction target unclear. Overall, the substantial dataset and empirical gains place this near acceptance, but uncertainty about evaluation independence and the unisolated headline claim makes the current balance borderline.

strengths: The combined dataset and modeling contribution addresses a meaningful bottleneck in VR sketch-conditioned shape generation. Collecting 900 human sketches from 15 participants across four categories, alongside 20,838 synthetic pairs with stroke sequences, provides a useful research resource beyond the previously public chair-only benchmark.

Table 2 shows substantial improvements over the evaluated baselines. Across the proposed dataset, F-score increases from 48.8 to 69.8 and CD decreases from 13.0 to 4.8 relative to Luo et al. Gains also hold on the independent 3DVRChair benchmark: F-score improves from 26.6 to 31.1 and CD decreases from 35.5 to 25.8. This external evaluation strengthens the evidence beyond the authors' own benchmark.

The architecture is technically coherent, and the ablations support the usefulness of its sequence representation and synthetic training. Removing index embeddings reduces F-score from 56.8 to 48.9; replacing the encoder with a point-cloud encoder reduces it to 30.8. The zero-shot results and adaptation curve provide encouraging evidence that the synthetic pipeline supplies useful supervision.

The qualitative examples show improved structural fidelity across several categories, while the partial-input experiments suggest practical value for progressive reconstruction. Architecture settings, training schedules, and measured inference time are reported. Overall, the demonstrated gains and resource contribution provide a stronger case for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The central claim about temporal drawing order is not cleanly isolated. The 'without ordering' ablation removes both stroke indices and within-stroke point indices, also removing information about stroke membership and local connectivity. It therefore demonstrates the value of structured sequence encoding, but does not establish that chronological stroke order itself is responsible. Comparisons preserving stroke structure while randomizing stroke order or reversing point direction would distinguish these explanations.

The new human benchmark uses tracing over visible target meshes with every point snapped onto the target surface. This is useful for controlled reconstruction, but differs materially from drawing a novel design without a reference shape. Its lower sketch-to-shape distance is partly guaranteed by acquisition rather than demonstrating more realistic inputs. The 3DVRChair results partially address this concern, but broad claims about real-world ideation and synthetic-to-freehand generalization remain stronger than the evidence.

The dataset split description does not establish whether the underlying ShapeNet mesh identities are disjoint between synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation, or whether participants are held out. This is an important uncertainty for interpreting generalization; it is not evidence that leakage occurred. Exact shape splits and the training provenance of the frozen VQ-VAE are needed to make the evaluation independently auditable.

The partial-sketch protocol pads the unseen remainder with MASK tokens and inserts SEP tokens using a stroke-length distribution. It is unclear whether padding uses the eventual complete sketch length, information unavailable during live drawing. Thus, Figures 6–7 support reconstruction from artificially truncated inputs more directly than an operational interactive completion system.

Methodological novelty is mainly an effective integration of established geometric extraction, SketchBERT-style encoding, and SDFusion. The resource and empirical results carry much of the contribution. Reproducibility and interpretation are also weakened by missing per-category results and variability estimates, and by Figure 5 showing 200 fine-tuning examples 'per category' although only chairs have that many. These reporting issues are secondary to the substantive evaluation concerns above.

strengths: The combined dataset, synthetic sketch pipeline, and reconstruction model provide a useful contribution to VR sketch-conditioned generation. Collecting 900 real sketches across four categories and generating 20,838 synthetic pairs addresses a practical supervision bottleneck.

Table 2 shows substantial improvements over retrained baselines on the proposed dataset: F-score increases from 48.8 to 69.8 and CD decreases from 13.0 to 4.8 against Luo et al. Improvements also transfer to the independent 3DVRChair benchmark, where F-score increases from 26.6 to 31.1 and CD decreases from 35.5 to 25.8.

The ablations support the value of the proposed representation beyond simply adopting a diffusion generator. Removing sequence indices reduces F-score from 56.8 to 48.9; replacing the encoder with SketchBERT or PointNet++ also degrades performance. Synthetic-only training and few-shot adaptation demonstrate practical value.

Evaluation extends beyond reference-guided reconstruction. The user study includes 20 free-hand sketches and 38 raters, with substantially higher correspondence ratings than Luo et al. Supplementary experiments examine partial inputs, order perturbations, unsnapped sketches, and sampling-speed tradeoffs.

Overall, the demonstrated reconstruction improvements and useful data contribution favor acceptance, despite reservations about the interpretation of temporal order and the completeness of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The central claim about human temporal order is only partly isolated. Removing both stroke and point indices also removes stroke membership and within-stroke structure, so Table 4 does not specifically establish the benefit of chronological stroke order. Table A-1 shows little effect from reversal and a smaller drop from scrambling strokes. These results support structured sequential encoding more directly than claims about capturing human design intent.

Dataset partitioning is insufficiently specified. The manuscript gives sketch counts but does not explicitly establish whether source ShapeNet identities are disjoint between synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation, or whether sketchers are held out. This is an important uncertainty for interpreting generalization; it is not evidence that leakage occurred.

Surface snapping makes the main benchmark substantially cleaner than ordinary VR input. The independent benchmark and free-hand study partly address this concern, but unsnapped and unseen-category generalization are supported primarily by selected visual examples. Strong claims of broad robustness exceed this evidence.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: the synthetic traversal initialization and point-resampling rules are unclear, and the diffusion description does not precisely specify its prediction target, noise schedule, or conditioning mechanism. Main quantitative results lack variation across training runs, while the user-study significance claim is not accompanied by an analysis accounting for repeated ratings of the same sketches.

Some reporting issues are readily correctable but affect interpretation. Figure 5 labels up to 200 real samples per category although only chairs have that many; Table A-2 labels latency-like values as samples/s. Its reported 6.33-to-2.26 change is approximately 2.8×, rather than over 3×, and does not establish real-time interaction.

strengths: The combined dataset and reconstruction framework constitute a useful contribution to VR sketch-conditioned 3D generation. Collecting 900 real sketches across four categories and generating 20,838 synthetic pairs addresses a concrete data bottleneck, even though the individual architectural components are established.

Table 2 provides substantial quantitative support: on the new dataset, F-score improves from 48.8 to 69.8 and CD×1000 decreases from 13.0 to 4.8 relative to Luo et al., with both methods trained on the synthetic data and fine-tuned on real sketches. Gains also hold on the independent 3DVRChair benchmark, although they are smaller: 26.6 to 31.1 F-score and 35.5 to 25.8 CD.

The ablations support the practical value of the proposed representation and training pipeline. Removing sequence indices reduces F-score from 56.8 to 48.9; removing augmentation reduces it to 49.0. The PointNet++ encoder comparison using the diffusion framework helps establish that improvements do not come solely from changing the generator.

Evidence extends beyond reference-guided reconstruction. The free-hand user study reports ratings of 3.60 versus 2.02 for Luo et al., and the supplement includes unsnapped inputs, partial sketches, and unseen categories, including visible failure cases. Together with the benchmark gains, this supports weak acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of 'order matters' is stronger than the experiments establish. Removing both stroke and point indices simultaneously removes stroke membership and within-stroke structure as well as temporal information. Table A-1 shows little effect from reversing stroke order and only a moderate F-score decrease from scrambling strokes (56.8 to 54.6). These results support structured sequence encoding more directly than human drawing chronology or design intent. A control preserving stroke identity and local connectivity while removing global temporal order is missing.

The dataset split description does not establish whether underlying ShapeNet objects are disjoint across synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation, or whether sketchers are held out. This does not demonstrate leakage, but it leaves uncertainty about whether synthetic-to-real results measure transfer to new shapes or new sketches of previously observed shapes. The pretrained VQ-VAE's training coverage is also unspecified.

Surface snapping makes the main benchmark substantially easier than unconstrained creative sketching: inputs are projected onto the target geometry. The lower sketch-to-shape distance in Table 1 is therefore partly a consequence of collection design, rather than independent evidence of benchmark quality. The free-hand study is valuable but contains only 20 free-hand sketches; unsnapped and unseen-category evaluations are qualitative. Broad robustness claims exceed this evidence.

The partial-sketch protocol pads the missing remainder of a completed sketch with MASK tokens and randomly inserts separators. It is unclear whether padding depends on the eventual full sketch length, which is unavailable during live drawing. Consequently, these experiments establish reconstruction from artificially masked sketches more clearly than performance in an online design workflow.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The diffusion description does not clearly distinguish clean-latent prediction from noise prediction, sequence sampling and length handling are underspecified, and quantitative ablations lack repeated-run uncertainty. Minor presentation errors include an inconsistent timing unit in Table A-2 and large percentage gains quoted in the 3DVRChair paragraph that actually describe the new dataset. These reporting issues are secondary to the substantive concerns above.

strengths: The paper makes a useful combined dataset and modeling contribution to VR sketch-conditioned shape generation: 20,838 synthetic sketch–shape pairs, 900 human-drawn pairs across four categories, and an encoder that preserves stroke structure. The automated synthesis pipeline addresses a meaningful data bottleneck.

The quantitative improvements are substantial. In Table 2, the proposed method achieves 69.8 F-score and 4.8 Chamfer distance versus Luo et al.'s 48.8 and 13.0 across the new dataset's categories. Improvements also extend to the existing 3DVRChair benchmark: 31.1 versus 26.6 F-score and 25.8 versus 35.5 Chamfer distance.

The ablations support the usefulness of the proposed representation and training choices. Removing sequence embeddings reduces F-score from 56.8 to 48.9, removing augmentation reduces it to 49.0, and substituting SketchBERT encoding yields 50.4. The point-cloud encoder comparison helps establish that the gains do not arise solely from adopting a diffusion generator.

Evaluation goes beyond reference-guided reconstruction. The 38-participant study favors the method on free-hand inputs, with mean correspondence ratings of 3.60 versus 2.02. Partial-sketch experiments, qualitative unsnapped inputs, and disclosed unseen-category failures provide useful evidence about practical behavior. Together, these results support weak acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The central temporal-order interpretation is stronger than the evidence establishes. Removing both stroke and point indices also removes explicit stroke membership and within-stroke structure, so this ablation does not isolate drawing chronology. Table A-1 shows almost unchanged performance under reversal and only a modest F-score reduction under stroke scrambling. The evidence supports structured sequential encoding more clearly than a claim that human temporal order captures design intent; the supplement acknowledges this distinction, but the main narrative remains stronger.

The dataset description does not explicitly establish whether underlying ShapeNet identities are disjoint between synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation. Calling the real sketches held out does not resolve whether their target shapes appeared during synthetic training. This is an important reproducibility and interpretation gap for the generalization results, although it does not establish that leakage occurred.

Surface snapping creates an unusually clean benchmark using privileged reference geometry. Its lower sketch-to-shape distance is partly guaranteed by construction and does not itself establish greater ecological validity. The free-hand user study meaningfully mitigates this concern, but it contains only 20 free-hand sketches; unsnapped and unseen-category evaluations are qualitative, limiting the breadth of supported deployment claims.

Architectural originality is moderate: the method combines established Fourier features, a SketchBERT-style transformer, SDFusion, and existing geometric processing components. Its strongest novelty lies in their task-specific integration and the dataset. The synthetic ordering heuristic is not validated as a model of human drawing behavior.

Several reporting details limit precise reproduction and interpretation: shape-level split identifiers, sequence-length handling, and the exact diffusion prediction target are insufficiently specified. Most quantitative comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, while the user study claims significance without describing a statistical test accounting for repeated ratings. Presentation errors also merit correction: the 3DVRChair discussion mixes in improvement percentages from the new dataset, and Table A-2 labels apparent seconds-per-sample measurements as samples/s.
